newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU banks on grain sales to E.Europe to cut costs.
newsitem.headline: EU banks on grain sales to E.Europe to cut costs.

text.p: The European Union, squeezed out of traditional grain outlets by rivals and facing pressure on subsidy budgets, is relying on Eastern Europe to help mop up a bumper harvest this year, European farm officials said.
Grain traders say Brussels is being too cautious with subsidies by using them only to close the gap between EU prices and lower -- but relatively firm -- prices in the U.S.
This is despite the loss of traditional wheat markets in North Africa, where business is being picked up at lower prices by Argentina and Australia, which also have big crops.
But EU officials have defended the policy of tracking U.S. prices and see Eastern Europe as a natural outlet given its proximity and generally poor harvests.
"We have a card to play on these destinations where we have some logistical advantages," an EU grain official said.
Poland was one of the EU's major targets this year, he said, with around a million tonnes of cereals already shipped or under way since the EU's grain year began on July 1.
Analysts say Central European wheat imports are likely to double during the current season to some two million tonnes. It is one of the few areas with poor output this year.
With transport costs low, the region has the added lure for the EU of needing less export subsidy to make deals happen.
A senior EU official said export refunds were coming under increasing pressure this year, especially after ministers put $1 billion aside to pay for dealing with mad cow disease.

"When you look at the extremely significant rise in our production and the export availabilities, we might have budget difficulties in the cereals sector," Michel Jacquot, the EU's FEOGA farm budget director, said.
The EU has a 16.16 billion Ecu arable budget for 1997, of which 366 million is put aside for cereals restitutions.
The budget has yet to be approved by the EU Parliament and Commission officials fear it will not keep pace with falling world grain prices.
EU member country sources said the budget assumed soft wheat export refunds of five Ecus per tonne for 1996/97 (July/June) whereas the latest export refunds were 19.45 Ecus.
Private traders peg the EU's export potential at nine million tonnes, of which four million tonnes has been done.

One European official believes budget problems will emerge in two to three months, meaning Brussels has an incentive to concentrate on nearby destinations such as Eastern Europe and keep subsidy spending down as far as possible.
Jacquot did not rule out some juggling between export subsidy spending and internal intervention storage as a way of managing costs if the budget stayed as it was.

Another official denied Brussels had already been tempted to cut a politically sensitive link with U.S. wheat prices to maintain markets. The last EU export subsidy award implied an EU wheat price in line with soft red winter, he said.
Although it doubled weekly exports to 400,000 tonnes on Thursday, the EU's export subsidy valued French wheat at $150 per tonne, he said.
This compared with U.S. soft red wheat at $149.
"We were clearly in line with Chicago. That suits us fine. We are very happy," he said, adding that the EU was on course to reach its export targets despite stiff competition this year.
